lines.text: Welcome to Fluent English. Today, we're learning the present perfect.
In this class, we will learn the present perfect together. We will listen, repeat, practice in pairs, and play some quick games.
First, you will talk about experiences.
Second, you will say what has just happened.
Third, you will say how long something has continued.
Fourth, you will ask and answer questions.
And fifth, you will choose between the present perfect and the simple past.
Use the chat, raise your hand, or speak out loud. Mistakes are fine. They help us learn. Let's begin.
First, meet our three friends.
Hi, I'm Maya.
Hi, I'm Daniel.
And I'm Sofia. We will help you today.
They will show you the grammar in real situations.
Warm up. Daniel and Maya will ask a question. Answer in your head, or in the chat: yes, I have, or no, I haven't.
Have you ever eaten sushi?
Yes, I have. I ate it in Tokyo.
Have you ever lost your phone?
No, I haven't. But I've lost my keys!
lines.say: No, I haven't. But [I've](/ˈaɪv/) lost my keys!

lines.text: Have you ever met a famous person?
Yes, I have. I met a singer last year.
Great. Today you will learn how to talk about experiences like these.
Daniel is at the office door. He's looking for his keys.
Where are my keys?
Oh no! I've lost my keys!
lines.say: Oh no! [I've](/ˈaɪv/) lost my keys!

lines.text: I lost my keys yesterday.
lines.say: I lost my keys yesterday.

lines.text: We name a finished time: yesterday. This is the simple past.
I've lost my keys.
lines.say: [I've](/ˈaɪv/) lost my keys.

lines.text: Now the focus is the present result. In this situation, we understand that the keys are missing now.
The present perfect connects the past to now.
Let's check. Listen to the question, think, and choose.
Which sentence names a finished time? One: I lost my keys yesterday.. Two: I've lost my keys..
lines.say: Which sentence names a finished time? One: I lost my keys yesterday.. Two: [I've](/ˈaɪv/) lost my keys..

lines.text: I lost my keys yesterday.. Yesterday is a finished time, so we use the simple past.
Which sentence focuses on the result now? One: I lost my keys yesterday.. Two: I've lost my keys..
lines.say: Which sentence focuses on the result now? One: I lost my keys yesterday.. Two: [I've](/ˈaɪv/) lost my keys..

lines.text: I've lost my keys.. I've lost my keys connects the past to now. In this situation, the keys are missing now.
lines.say: [I've](/ˈaɪv/) lost my keys.. [I've](/ˈaɪv/) lost my keys connects the past to now. In this situation, the keys are missing now.

lines.text: Now, repeat after me. First, the simple past. Then, the present perfect.
I lost my keys yesterday.
I've lost my keys.
lines.say: [I've](/ˈaɪv/) lost my keys.

lines.text: The form is: subject, plus have or has, plus the past participle.
She has finished.
I, you, we, and they use have. He, she, and it use has.
The past participle is the third verb form. It is not always the simple past.
Work, worked, worked. See, saw, seen. Go, went, gone. Be, was, been. Eat, ate, eaten.
I've finished. She's finished.
lines.say: [I've](/ˈaɪv/) finished. She's finished.

lines.text: Here, apostrophe s means has. It can also mean is, so check the next word.
Quick check one. She, blank, finished the report. Have, has, or does?
Has. She is third person singular: she has finished.
Quick drill. I will say a subject. You say have or has. Ready?
I
have
you
have
he
has
she
has
it
has
we
have
they
have
Maya
has
my friends
have
my sister
has
Well done. He, she, and it use has. Everyone else uses have.
Now, listen and repeat. Notice the three parts: subject, have or has, and the past participle.
I have finished my homework.
You have worked hard.
He has eaten lunch.
She has seen that movie.
We have been to Mexico.
They have bought a new car.
Four quick questions. Think first, then choose.
Number one. My brother, blank, visited Spain. have, has, or does?
Has. My brother is he, so we use has.
Number two. Maya and Daniel, blank, finished. have, has, or does?
Have. Maya and Daniel is they, so we use have.
Number three. I've, blank, that song before. heard, hear, or hearing?
lines.say: Number three. [I've](/ˈaɪv/), blank, that song before. heard, hear, or hearing?

lines.text: Heard. After have, we need the past participle: heard.
Number four. She has, blank, her keys. lost, lose, or losing?
Lost. Has plus the past participle: lost.
Regular verbs add e d. But we say e d in three different ways. Listen and repeat.
Sound t. Worked. Watched. Helped. Cooked.
Sound d. Played. Lived. Cleaned. Opened.
Sound id. Wanted. Needed. Visited. Decided.
After t or d, e d is an extra syllable. Everywhere else, it is just t or d.
Now, irregular verbs. They do not add e d. Group one: many participles end in e n.
eat, ate, eaten.
see, saw, seen.
give, gave, given.
take, took, taken.
write, wrote, written.
break, broke, broken.
Your turn. I say the base verb. You say the past participle.
eat
eaten
see
seen
give
given
take
taken
write
written
break
broken
Group two: very common verbs. Learn these first.
go, went, gone.
do, did, done.
be, was or were, been.
have, had, had.
make, made, made.
say, said, said.
go
gone
do
done
be
been
have
had
make
made
say
said
Group three: the simple past and the past participle are the same.
buy, bought, bought.
bring, brought, brought.
find, found, found.
lose, lost, lost.
leave, left, left.
meet, met, met.
buy
bought
bring
brought
find

lose
lost
leave
left
meet
met
Group four: some verbs do not change, or they change only a little.
put, put, put.
cut, cut, cut.
read, red, red. The spelling is the same, but the sound changes.
run, ran, run.
come, came, come.
hit, hit, hit.
put
put

run

come

Participle quiz. Eight questions. Think first, then choose.
Number one. She has, blank, a letter. wrote, written, or write?
Written. Written is the past participle of write.
Number two. We've, blank, to the park. went, gone, or go?
lines.say: Number two. [We've](/wˈiv/), blank, to the park. went, gone, or go?

lines.text: Gone. Gone is the past participle of go.
Number three. He has, blank, his homework. did, done, or do?
Done. Done is the past participle of do.
Number four. They've, blank, a new house. bought, buy, or buying?
lines.say: Number four. [They've](/ðˈeɪv/), blank, a new house. bought, buy, or buying?

lines.text: Bought. Bought is the past participle of buy.
Number five. I've, blank, Maria twice. met, meet, or meeting?
lines.say: Number five. [I've](/ˈaɪv/), blank, Maria twice. met, meet, or meeting?

lines.text: Met. Met is the past participle of meet.
Number six. Have you, blank, that movie? saw, seen, or see?
Seen. Seen is the past participle of see.
Number seven. She has, blank, the window. broke, broken, or break?
Broken. Broken is the past participle of break.
Number eight. I have, blank, to Italy three times. been, was, or be?
Been. Been is the past participle of be.
In speech, we usually use short forms. Listen and repeat.
I have, I've.
lines.say: I have, [I've](/ˈaɪv/).

lines.text: you have, you've.
lines.say: you have, [you've](/jˈuv/).

lines.text: we have, we've.
lines.say: we have, [we've](/wˈiv/).

lines.text: they have, they've.
lines.say: they have, [they've](/ðˈeɪv/).

lines.text: he has, he's.
she has, she's.
it has, it's.
Careful: apostrophe s can mean has or is. Check the next word.
Now you say the short form.
She has finished.
She's finished.
I have eaten.
I've eaten.
lines.say: [I've](/ˈaɪv/) eaten.

lines.text: They have arrived.
They've arrived.
lines.say: [They've](/ðˈeɪv/) arrived.

lines.text: He has gone.
He's gone.
We have started.
We've started.
lines.say: [We've](/wˈiv/) started.

lines.text: For negatives, put not after have or has. Haven't. Hasn't.
I haven't finished. She hasn't finished.
For questions, put have or has before the subject.
Have you finished? Has she finished?
We do not use do or does to make these questions.
Make these sentences negative. Use haven't or hasn't.
I have finished.
I haven't finished.
She has called.
She hasn't called.
They have arrived.
They haven't arrived.
He has eaten.
He hasn't eaten.
We have seen it.
We haven't seen it.
Now make questions. Put have or has first.
You have finished.
Have you finished?
She has called.
Has she called?
They have arrived.
Have they arrived?
He has eaten.
Has he eaten?
It has stopped.
Has it stopped?
Have you eaten lunch?
Yes, I have.
Has Sofia called?
No, she hasn't.
Give the short answer. Yes or no, plus the subject, plus have or has.
Have you eaten? Yes.
Yes, I have.
Has she called? No.
No, she hasn't.
Have they arrived? Yes.
Yes, they have.
Has he finished? No.
No, he hasn't.
Has it started? Yes.
Yes, it has.
With question words, put have or has next, before the subject.
What have you done? How long have you lived here?
Listen and repeat. Question word, then have or has, then the subject.
What have you done?
Where have you been?
How long have you lived here?
Who have you called?
Quick check two. Maya has already, blank, lunch. Ate, eaten, or eat?
Eaten. After has, we need the past participle: has eaten.
Four more questions about negatives and questions.
Number one. She, blank, finished yet. hasn't, haven't, or doesn't?
Hasn't. She is he, she, or it, so we use hasn't.
Number two. blank, you ever visited Canada? Have, Has, or Do?
Have. Have comes first, before the subject you.
Has he finished? Number three. Yes, he, blank, . has, does, or is?
Has. A short answer repeats has.
Number four. How long, blank, they lived here? have, has, or did?
Have. They uses have, and lived is the past participle.
Pair work time. Work with a partner. Partner one asks the questions. Partner two answers with a short answer.
Then I will say, switch roles, and you change. You have three minutes. Start now.
Switch roles!
Time's up. Great job. Let's come back together.
Use one: experience up to now. We don't say when.
Have you ever visited Canada?
Yes, I have. I visited Canada in 2022.
lines.say: Yes, I have. I visited Canada in twenty twenty-two.

lines.text: First, the experience: present perfect. Then a finished time: simple past.
Never means: not at any time, up to now.
I've never visited Canada.
lines.say: [I've](/ˈaɪv/) never visited Canada.

lines.text: Four useful words for experience.
Ever means at any time in your life. We use it in questions.
Never means not at any time. We use it with a positive verb, not with not.
We can also say once, twice, or three times.
And before means, at some time in the past.
Repeat after me.
Have you ever visited Canada?
I've never visited Canada.
lines.say: [I've](/ˈaɪv/) never visited Canada.

lines.text: I've visited Canada twice.
lines.say: [I've](/ˈaɪv/) visited Canada twice.

lines.text: I've been there before.
lines.say: [I've](/ˈaɪv/) been there before.

lines.text: Now you ask the question. I say an idea. You ask, have you ever, plus the past participle.
Eat sushi.
Have you ever eaten sushi?
See a whale.
Have you ever seen a whale?
Ride a horse.
Have you ever ridden a horse?
Meet a famous person.
Have you ever met a famous person?
Lose your phone.
Have you ever lost your phone?
Break a bone.
Have you ever broken a bone?
Experience quiz. Four questions.
Number one. blank, you ever eaten snails? Have, Has, or Do?
Have. Have comes before you, and eaten is the past participle.
She doesn't know the city. Number two. Maya has, blank, been to Paris. never, ever, or yet?
Never. Never means not at any time.
It was great both times. Number three. I've visited London, blank. twice, ever, or never?
lines.say: It was great both times. Number three. [I've](/ˈaɪv/) visited London, blank. twice, ever, or never?

lines.text: Twice. Twice means two times.
Number four. blank, she ever met a famous person? Has, Have, or Is?
Has. She uses has.
Pair work. Ask your partner, have you ever, and one of these ideas. If the answer is yes, ask, when was that? The answer uses the simple past.
Partner one asks first. After two minutes, I will say switch. You have four minutes.
Switch roles!
Time's up. Well done.
Now, tell the class about your partner. Use has. For example: Ana has visited Brazil.
Volunteers, please. Speak now, or write in the chat.
Use two: a recent action with a result now.
Have you finished yet?
Yes! I've already finished the report.
lines.say: Yes! [I've](/ˈaɪv/) already finished the report.

lines.text: The report is finished, and it is ready now.
Already goes before the participle. Yet goes at the end.
I haven't finished yet.
Three small words for recent results: just, already, and yet.
Just means a very short time ago.
Already means earlier than expected. It goes before the participle.
Yet goes at the end of questions.
And in negatives, yet means, until now.
Repeat after me.
I've just arrived.
lines.say: [I've](/ˈaɪv/) just arrived.

lines.text: She's already left.
Have you eaten yet?
He hasn't called yet.
Listen to Maya and Daniel at the office. Listen for yet, just, and already.
Daniel, have you finished the report yet?
Not yet. I've just started the last page.
lines.say: Not yet. [I've](/ˈaɪv/) just started the last page.

lines.text: Have you called the client?
Yes, I have. I've already called him twice.
lines.say: Yes, I have. [I've](/ˈaɪv/) already called him twice.

lines.text: Great! Then you haven't forgotten anything.
I hope not!
Yet is in the question. Just and already go before the participle.
Result quiz. Five questions.
I did it two minutes ago. Number one. I've, blank, finished. just, yet, or ever?
lines.say: I did it two minutes ago. Number one. [I've](/ˈaɪv/), blank, finished. just, yet, or ever?

lines.text: Just. Just means a very short time ago.
Number two. Have you finished the report, blank, ? yet, ever, or never?
Yet. Yet goes at the end of a question.
Do you want some lunch? Number three. No, thanks. I've, blank, eaten. already, yet, or ever?
lines.say: Do you want some lunch? Number three. No, thanks. [I've](/ˈaɪv/), blank, eaten. already, yet, or ever?

lines.text: Already. Already goes before the participle.
We are still waiting. Number four. He hasn't called, blank. yet, already, or just?
Yet. In a negative sentence, yet goes at the end.
You can't catch it. Number five. The train has, blank, left. just, yet, or ever?
Just. Just means a very short time ago.
Look at the situation. Say a sentence about the result. Use the present perfect.
Daniel can't open the door. Use the verb lose.
He's lost his keys.
Maya's desk is clean. Use the verb finish.
She's finished her work.
The plate is empty. Use the verb eat.
He's eaten everything.
The suitcase is at the door. Use the verb pack.
She's packed her suitcase.
The cake is on the table. Use the verb bake.
They've baked a cake.
lines.say: [They've](/ðˈeɪv/) baked a cake.

lines.text: Use three: a situation that began in the past and continues now.
I've known her for five years.
lines.say: [I've](/ˈaɪv/) known her for five years.

lines.text: And she's lived here since 2021.
lines.say: And she's lived here since twenty twenty-one.

lines.text: For introduces a length of time. Since introduces the starting point.
Careful: for and since do not always mean present perfect. A finished situation uses the simple past.
She lived in Paris for two years.
Quick check three. Daniel has worked here, blank, 2019. For, or since?
lines.say: Quick check three. Daniel has worked here, blank, twenty nineteen. For, or since?

lines.text: Since. 2019 is the starting point, not a length of time.
lines.say: Since. Twenty nineteen is the starting point, not a length of time.

lines.text: Game time. For or since? I show a time expression. Is it a length of time, for, or a starting point, since?
five years
For.

lines.say: twenty nineteen

lines.text: Since.
Monday
Since.
three days
For.
last year
Since.
a long time
For.
I was a child
Since.
ten minutes
For.
yesterday
Since.
two hours
For.
To ask about a period up to now, we say, how long have you.
Answer with for, and a length of time.
Or answer with since, and a starting point.
Repeat after me.
How long have you lived here?
I've lived here for three years.
lines.say: [I've](/ˈaɪv/) lived here for three years.

lines.text: I've lived here since 2022.
lines.say: [I've](/ˈaɪv/) lived here since twenty twenty-two.

lines.text: Now you answer with a full sentence. Use for, or since.
How long have you lived here? Five years.
I've lived here for five years.
lines.say: [I've](/ˈaɪv/) lived here for five years.

lines.text: How long have you studied English? Since January.
I've studied English since January.
lines.say: [I've](/ˈaɪv/) studied English since January.

lines.text: How long has she worked here? Two months.
She has worked here for two months.
How long have they been married? Since 2021.
lines.say: How long have they been married? Since twenty twenty-one.

lines.text: They've been married since 2021.
lines.say: [They've](/ðˈeɪv/) been married since twenty twenty-one.

lines.text: How long has he had that car? Ten years.
He has had that car for ten years.
Three quick questions.
Number one. She has worked here, blank, six months. for, since, or during?
For. Six months is a length of time. Use for.
Number two. We've known each other, blank, we were students. since, for, or from?
lines.say: Number two. [We've](/wˈiv/) known each other, blank, we were students. since, for, or from?

lines.text: Since. We were students is a starting point. Use since.
Number three. How long, blank, you studied English? have, do, or are?
Have. How long, have, you, and the past participle studied.
Pair work. Ask, how long have you, and one of these ideas. Answer with for, or since.
Partner one asks first. When I say switch, change roles. You have three minutes.
Switch roles!
Time's up. Great speaking.
Use four: a period that is not finished yet, like today, this week, or this year.
I've had two meetings so far today.
lines.say: [I've](/ˈaɪv/) had two meetings so far today.

lines.text: Today is not over, so we use the present perfect. Yesterday is finished, so we use the simple past.
I had two meetings yesterday.
Advanced note: the speaker's view matters. If you see today as finished, the simple past is also possible.
Remember: with a finished time, like yesterday, last week, or in 2022, use the simple past.
lines.say: Remember: with a finished time, like yesterday, last week, or in twenty twenty-two, use the simple past.

lines.text: I saw her yesterday.
Not: I've seen her yesterday.
lines.say: Not: [I've](/ˈaɪv/) seen her yesterday.

lines.text: Quick check four. Sofia's trip was last summer. We, blank, Canada last summer. Visited, or have visited?
Visited. Last summer is a finished time, so we use the simple past.
A quick map of time words.
Words like ever, never, already, yet, and just usually go with the present perfect.
So do for and since, when the situation continues now.
But words for a finished time, like yesterday, last week, in twenty nineteen, or two days ago, go with the simple past.
Today, this week, and this year can go either way. The speaker's view matters.
Listen to Sofia and Daniel. Notice how the tense changes.
I've visited Canada three times.
lines.say: [I've](/ˈaɪv/) visited Canada three times.

lines.text: Really? When did you first go?
I went there in 2019, and I loved it.
lines.say: I went there in twenty nineteen, and I loved it.

lines.text: Have you been back since then?
Yes. We went again last summer.
First, the present perfect, for an experience. Then, the simple past, for the finished times.
Six questions. Look for the time words.
Number one. I, blank, to Paris in 2019. went, have been, or have gone?
lines.say: Number one. I, blank, to Paris in twenty nineteen. went, have been, or have gone?

lines.text: Went. In twenty nineteen is a finished time. Use the simple past.
Number two. She, blank, here since 2021. has lived, lived, or is living?
lines.say: Number two. She, blank, here since twenty twenty-one. has lived, lived, or is living?

lines.text: Has lived. Since twenty twenty-one: the situation continues, so use the present perfect.
Number three. We, blank, that movie last night. saw, have seen, or are seeing?
Saw. Last night is a finished time. Use the simple past.
Number four. They, blank, married two years ago. got, have got, or have gotten?
Got. Two years ago is a finished time. Use the simple past.
He still works here. Number five. He, blank, here for five years. has worked, worked, or was working?
Has worked. He still works here, so we use the present perfect.
Number six. When, blank, you finish the report? did, have, or has?
Did. With when, we ask about a finished time. Use did.
American English note: the simple past is also common with just, already, and yet. Both are normal.
I just ate. I already finished. Did you finish yet?
Where's Sofia?
She's gone to London.
Gone: she is away, on her trip.
She's been to London.
Been: she visited London at some time. This is an experience.
Three quick questions about been and gone.
Where's Daniel? He'll be back soon. Number one. He's, blank, to the bank. gone, or been?
Gone. Gone means he is away now.
It's a beautiful city. Number two. I've, blank, to Rome twice. been, or gone?
lines.say: It's a beautiful city. Number two. [I've](/ˈaɪv/), blank, to Rome twice. been, or gone?

lines.text: Been. Been means a visit, and then I came back.
Sofia isn't here. Number three. She's, blank, to London. gone, or been?
Gone. Gone means she is there now, on her trip.
One more related form is the present perfect continuous. It can also describe situations that continue, but it is a separate form, and it is not in this lesson.
Game time. I show a sentence with one mistake. Find it, and fix it.
Find the mistake. I've seen her yesterday.
lines.say: Find the mistake. [I've](/ˈaɪv/) seen her yesterday.

lines.text: I saw her yesterday. Yesterday is a finished time. Use the simple past.
Find the mistake. He have finished.
He has finished. He needs has.
Find the mistake. I've lived here since five years.
lines.say: Find the mistake. [I've](/ˈaɪv/) lived here since five years.

lines.text: I've lived here for five years. Five years is a length of time. Use for.
lines.say: [I've](/ˈaɪv/) lived here for five years. Five years is a length of time. Use for.

lines.text: Find the mistake. They haven't call yet.
They haven't called yet. After haven't, use the past participle.
Find the mistake. Have you eat lunch?
Have you eaten lunch? Eaten is the past participle.
Find the mistake. She's visited Paris last year.
She visited Paris last year. Last year is a finished time. Use the simple past.
Find the mistake. Did you ever been to Japan?
Have you ever been to Japan? Use have, plus the past participle.
Another game. I say a sentence. Is it the present perfect, or the simple past?
I've just finished.
lines.say: [I've](/ˈaɪv/) just finished.

lines.text: Present perfect.
We went there in 2019.
lines.say: We went there in twenty nineteen.

lines.text: Simple past.
She's never been to Asia.
Present perfect.
I finished at noon.
Simple past.
Have you eaten yet?
Present perfect.
Did you call him yesterday?
Simple past.
He's lived here since 2020.
lines.say: He's lived here since twenty twenty.

lines.text: Present perfect.
They arrived two hours ago.
Simple past.
Quiz show! Ten questions. Think, answer in the chat, and see if you are right.
Number one. We, blank, in this city since 2020. have lived, lived, or live?
lines.say: Number one. We, blank, in this city since twenty twenty. have lived, lived, or live?

lines.text: Have lived. Since twenty twenty means the situation continues. Use the present perfect.
Number two. blank, you ever been to London? Have, Did, or Are?
Have. Have you ever been.
Number three. Maya, blank, the report yet. hasn't finished, didn't finished, or haven't finished?
Hasn't finished. Maya is she. Hasn't finished.
Number four. I, blank, breakfast at seven yesterday. had, have had, or has had?
Had. Yesterday is a finished time. Use the simple past.
Number five. She's, blank, to Rome three times. been, gone, or went?
Been. Been, for a visit.
Number six. I haven't seen him, blank, Monday. since, for, or from?
Since. Monday is a starting point. Use since.
Number seven. We've, blank, eaten. We're full. already, yet, or ever?
lines.say: Number seven. [We've](/wˈiv/), blank, eaten. We're full. already, yet, or ever?

lines.text: Already. Already goes before the participle.
Number eight. How long, blank, you known her? have, did, or do?
Have. How long have you known her.
Number nine. I, blank, him last week. saw, have seen, or has seen?
Saw. Last week is a finished time. Use the simple past.
Number ten. She has, blank, in Canada for ten years. lived, live, or living?
Lived. Has plus the past participle.
Listen to Sofia and Maya. How many present perfect sentences can you hear?
Maya! I haven't seen you for ages!
Sofia! Have you been away?
Yes, I have. I've just come back from Canada.
lines.say: Yes, I have. [I've](/ˈaɪv/) just come back from Canada.

lines.text: Wow! Have you ever visited Canada before?
No, I've never been there. It was my first time.
lines.say: No, [I've](/ˈaɪv/) never been there. It was my first time.

lines.text: How long have you been back?
Since Monday. I've already unpacked, but I haven't called my family yet.
lines.say: Since Monday. [I've](/ˈaɪv/) already unpacked, but I haven't called my family yet.

lines.text: Did you hear ever, never, just, already, yet, for, and since? Our friends used them all.
Role play time. Imagine you meet a friend after a long time. Use these ideas, and speak naturally.
You have four minutes. I will say switch in the middle. Start now.
Switch roles!
Time's up. Wonderful. I heard great sentences.
Now, a few volunteers. Tell the class one sentence about yourself with I've, and one sentence about your partner with has.
lines.say: Now, a few volunteers. Tell the class one sentence about yourself with [I've](/ˈaɪv/), and one sentence about your partner with has.

lines.text: Let's review. Subject, plus have or has, plus the past participle.
Use it for experience, a recent result, a situation that continues, and an unfinished time.
For a finished time, use the simple past.
Last activity: your exit ticket. Four questions, one for each use. Check what you remember.
Number one. I, blank, never visited Canada. have, has, or am?
Have. I have never visited. Experience.
Here is the report. Number two. I've, blank, finished. just, ever, or since?
lines.say: Here is the report. Number two. [I've](/ˈaɪv/), blank, finished. just, ever, or since?

lines.text: Just. Just means a very short time ago. Recent result.
Number three. She has lived here, blank, 2021. since, for, or ago?
lines.say: Number three. She has lived here, blank, twenty twenty-one. since, for, or ago?

lines.text: Since. Since gives the starting point. Still true.
Number four. We, blank, to the beach last Sunday. went, have been, or have gone?
Went. Last Sunday is a finished time. Simple past.
Now it's your turn! Say three sentences. Something you've done today. A place you've never visited. Someone you've known for years.
lines.say: Now it's your turn! Say three sentences. Something [you've](/jˈuv/) done today. A place [you've](/jˈuv/) never visited. Someone [you've](/jˈuv/) known for years.

lines.text: Great work. See you in the next lesson!
